title: Abram Leaves Home on a Promise
overview: God calls Abram to leave everything familiar for a new land with huge promises attached, and then Abram's fear in Egypt nearly costs his wife dearly.

parts.label: The call and the promise (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: God tells Abram to leave his homeland, relatives and family home for a land not yet named, and promises to make him a great people, bless him, and bless every people on earth through him. Christians later read that last line as pointing ahead to Jesus, through whom they believe the blessing reaches the whole world.

parts.label: Abram sets out (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: At seventy five, Abram leaves Harran with his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, their goods, and the people who had joined his household there, likely servants and workers. The journey to Canaan is told briefly: they set out, and they arrived.

parts.label: Altars in a land already lived in (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: The text notes that Canaanites already live there, so the promise to give this land to Abram's descendants is made while it still belongs to others. Building altars at Shechem and near Bethel was an open act of worship, honoring the LORD and showing trust in that promise as Abram moved south toward the dry Negev region.

parts.label: Famine and a fearful plan (vv. 10-13)
parts.note: A severe famine drives Abram to Egypt, and he fears the Egyptians will kill him to take his beautiful wife. He asks Sarai to say she is his sister, which a later chapter says was partly true, but here it is used to deceive, protecting him by putting her at risk.

parts.label: Sarai taken by Pharaoh (vv. 14-16)
parts.note: Pharaoh's officials praise Sarai, she is taken into his household as a wife, and Abram is given livestock and servants because of her. The story never tells us what Sarai herself felt or said.

parts.label: God steps in (vv. 17-20)
parts.note: The LORD strikes Pharaoh's household with serious diseases, and Pharaoh, the outsider, sharply rebukes Abram for lying before sending him away with Sarai and everything he owns. The text does not explain why Pharaoh's household suffered for Abram's lie, but it is frank that the man given the promise failed badly and the promise was protected anyway.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether God's promises of land and nationhood here still apply in a direct way to the Jewish people today or are fulfilled more broadly through Jesus and the worldwide church.
think: What makes a person brave enough to leave the familiar for something they cannot yet see, yet still capable of acting out of fear at someone else's expense soon after?
